chief_complaint: dome-shaped waxy papules with central dimple in child
hpi_details: 5-year-old girl is brought in by her mother for a rash on her trunk and axillae that has been present for 3 months. The lesions are asymptomatic, firm, dome-shaped, flesh-colored papules, many of which have a distinct central indentation (umbilication).
ideas: Her mother thinks the bumps might be water warts she picked up from other children at the community swimming pool.
concerns: Her mother is worried that the bumps will spread to her face and leave permanent scars before kindergarten school photos next month.
expectations: Her mother hopes the doctor can prescribe a gentle cream or freeze them off today so they disappear quickly.
social_hx: Lives with family; no relevant exposure history reported

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Molluscum Contagiosum is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Molluscum Contagiosum: Reassurance (self-limiting), cryotherapy or Cantharidin, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: dome-shaped waxy papules with central dimple in child
Key HPI features: A 5-year-old girl has asymptomatic firm, dome-shaped, flesh-colored papules with central umbilication on the trunk and axillae for 3 months.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Molluscum Contagiosum.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Molluscum Contagiosum.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Warts without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Extensive, unusually large, or rapidly spreading lesions, especially in an adult — consider underlying immunosuppression (HIV).
management_principles: Plan for Molluscum Contagiosum: Reassurance (self-limiting), cryotherapy or Cantharidin
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: dome-shaped waxy papules with central dimple in child

5-year-old girl is brought in by her mother for a rash on her trunk and axillae that has been present for 3 months. The lesions are asymptomatic, firm, dome-shaped, flesh-colored papules, many of which have a distinct central indentation (umbilication).
reference_soap.objective: Skin exam reveals 15-20 discrete, 2-5 mm, firm, pearly, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication distributed in the bilateral axillae and lateral trunk. No surrounding erythema.
reference_soap.plan: Reassure parents that this is a benign, self-limiting viral skin infection. Observation is the preferred management for children. Alternatively, can offer topical Cantharidin, cryotherapy, or curettage if lesions are severely bothersome or spreading rapidly.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Molluscum Contagiosum
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Molluscum Contagiosum
Implement evidence-based management plan: Reassurance (self-limiting), cryotherapy or Cantharidin

teaching.one_liner: A benign poxvirus infection causing dome-shaped waxy papules with a central dimple in a child.
red_flags: Extensive, unusually large, or rapidly spreading lesions, especially in an adult — consider underlying immunosuppression (HIV)
Signs of secondary bacterial infection (surrounding cellulitis, pain, pus)
Periocular lesions with conjunctivitis — needs ophthalmology evaluation

must_ask.say: Do the bumps have a dimple in the center?
How long has this been going on?
Has the child been around others with similar bumps?

history.answer: My daughter has these small bumps on her body with little dimples in the middle, and they've been there for about three months.
They first showed up about three months ago on the side of her chest, and gradually more appeared in her armpits.
They are mostly under both of her armpits and along the sides of her trunk.
They look like tiny, smooth, shiny bumps with a small dent right in the center.
No, she never complains of itching, burning, or pain, and she doesn't scratch them at all.
No, they stay in the same spots constantly and do not disappear or come and go.
She has never had skin bumps like this before.
No, she has not had any fever, chills, fatigue, or body aches.
No, there are no sores or blisters in her mouth, around her eyes, or on her private parts.
No, her skin is not peeling, and there are no purple spots or bruises.
No, she has never had lip swelling, tongue swelling, or trouble breathing.
She hasn't taken any prescription medicines, antibiotics, or pain medications recently.
No, we haven't changed her laundry detergent, soap, lotion, or bath products.
No, neither her older brother nor my husband and I have any bumps like this.
No bug bites that I know of, but she does go to weekly swimming lessons at the public pool.
No, she has never had eczema, asthma, or food allergies.
No, her joints are fine and her fingernails look completely normal.
I haven't applied any steroid creams, antifungal ointments, or over-the-counter medicine to them.
I thought maybe she caught some kind of water warts from the community pool, since a few kids in her swim class had little bumps.
I'm terrified they're going to spread all over her face and leave scars just in time for her kindergarten picture day next month.
I was hoping you could prescribe a quick cream or freeze them off right now so we can get rid of them.
She has been very healthy and has no chronic medical illnesses.
She has never had surgery and has never stayed in a hospital.
She is not taking any regular medications or vitamin supplements.
She does not have any known allergies to medicines.
No one smokes in our home or anywhere around our children.
She lives at home with her father, her older brother, and me.
No one in our family has chronic skin disorders or immune problems.
She was born full term through a normal delivery without any birth complications.
She is growing normally and is fully up to date on all her childhood immunizations.
She goes to preschool on weekdays and has normal contact with other kids.

exam.finding: Well-nourished, well-appearing child sitting comfortably on the examination table in no acute distress.
Blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, pulse 96 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, body temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Conjunctivae are clear without discharge or injection, and sclerae are non-icteric.
Oral mucosa and pharynx are clear, pink, and moist with no ulcerations, vesicles, or mucosal lesions.
No palpable anterior or posterior cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Axillary vaults demonstrate dome-shaped papules consistent with skin exam, but no axillary lymphadenopathy or tenderness is present.
Approximately 15 to 20 discrete, 2 to 5 mm, firm, pearly, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication over the bilateral axillae and lateral trunk without surrounding erythema or warmth.
External genital area is clear without papules, ulcers, erythema, or discharge.
